newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-Spain's May jobless drops, more falls seen.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Spain's May jobless drops, more falls seen.

text.p: Spain's unemployment rate dropped once again in May and the pace of improvement quickened, but the nation still faces a daunting task to rein in Europe's highest jobless rate, economists said on Monday.
Registered unemployment fell to 13.26 percent in May, down from 13.61 percent in April and from 14.36 percent a year earlier, the Labour Ministry reported.
The number of jobless fell by 57,866 -- well above a typical May figure -- to 2.12 million people.
"The trend is extremely favourable. But there's a long way to go," said Henrik Lumholdt, chief economist at the Bank of America in Madrid.

Spain's one-year-old minority conservative government has made dramatic progress in containing inflation and the budget deficit and has shaped up the country for the launch of Europe's single currency scheduled for 1999.
But until recently, unemployment had appeared intractable.
"The pace of declines has accelerated down from 14.1 percent in January," said William Thornhill, senior economist at Technical Data.

"The decline has...to do with economic revival and seasonal factors. Nevertheless, the decline so far this year suggests the government estimates of 200,000 (jobs to be created this year) will be exceeded. We're going for 250,000," he said.
At the start of the year, Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar vowed 1997 would be the year of the job and the government pledged to create 200,000 net new jobs.
Spain's actual job-creation trend has been even better than the unemployment numbers suggest, economists say, given dramatic growth in the working population.
Spain has been creating jobs at a three percent pace over the last two years, well above general economic growth of 2.3 percent in 1996 and 2.8 percent in 1995, Lumholdt said.

The improvement is particularly remarkable because of the growth of the labour pool. Spain faces both a long-term influx of women into the workforce and the re-entry of those who see the economic recovery as a chance to get back into work.
"The outlook is good. Spain is impressive if job growth is what has to happen," Lumholdt said. "It's (Spain) moving very fast, but it has a very bad past record."
Spain's heavy unemployment is in large part a legacy of fascist dictator Francisco Franco, who died in 1975, having set up a labour framework that gave workers near total security.

While this presented no problems during periods of economic expansion, as growth slowed high dismissal costs discouraged employment and registered joblessness rose steadily to a peak of 17.1 percent in 1994.
But reforms in 1984 and particularly, 1994, are beginning to make a difference. And economists expect the latest reform, which took effect on May 17, will also bring improvement.
"I think (unemployment declines) will accelerate in the third and fourth quarter as the effects of the labour reform (show through)," Thornhill said.
